title: A Vision for Teaching English
author: David Didau
summary: Didau presents the vision statement for the TransformED Northern Ireland Curriculum 2028 English framework, which he helped develop, arguing that English must be conceived as the study of language both as a means of living and as a tool for human thought — not merely a skills-acquisition subject. The framework positions English as a gateway to human experience through literature, grounding pupils in a cumulative, knowledge-rich curriculum that deliberately teaches vocabulary, phonological awareness, and text structure rather than assuming these will emerge naturally from exposure. Didau emphasises that reading for pleasure is not the starting condition but a long-term outcome of a curriculum that first builds competence and shared cultural entitlement. The vision statement articulates four entitlements: knowledge that helps pupils understand the world, language that enables precision of expression, literature that illuminates human experience, and habits of attention that support thoughtful engagement.
points: English must be framed as the study of language as a means of living and a tool for human thought — not a collection of transferable skills — placing linguistic and literary knowledge at the centre rather than the periphery of the subject.

Reading for pleasure is a long-term outcome of a competence-building curriculum, not a prerequisite: the curriculum must first develop fluency, vocabulary, and background knowledge before genuine readerly pleasure becomes accessible to all students.

Vocabulary is treated as a conceptual tool in this framework: as vocabulary expands, so does the reach of thought, which is why it must be taught deliberately across all stages, not left to incidental acquisition.

A cumulative approach — in which phonological awareness and decoding automaticity are prioritised in Foundation and Key Stage 1 before higher-order literary analysis — is essential to prevent the achievement gap from widening across the school career.

Wide reading across time, genre, and tradition gives students the intertextual knowledge to recognise that stories are not isolated but belong to a shared cultural landscape in which ideas are inherited, contested, and refined.
quotes: English is the study of language both as a means of living and as a tool for human thought. A high-quality English curriculum allows pupils to participate fully in the world and fosters their sense of belonging within it.

Through confident reading and attentive listening, pupils not only allow others to communicate successfully with them, they enter the wider conversation in which literature records and reshapes human experience. The study of English becomes a gateway to deep wells of thought and experience beyond their own.

The intensely personal pleasure of immersion in the flow of well-crafted prose makes a text a place to live inside and where a pupil makes meaning at their own pace. Whether through the narrative tension and fully imagined world of a novel or through an intricately crafted argument, a literary text captivates the readers mind.

Vocabulary runs through every aspect of the subject. Words function as conceptual tools that enable pupils to make finer distinctions, perceive pattern and hold more complex ideas in mind. As vocabulary expands, so does the reach of thought.

A cumulative approach shapes the teaching of reading, writing and spoken language. Reading fluency and disciplinary knowledge must be built step by step. In Foundation and Key Stage 1, this means that phonological awareness and decoding ability are priorities until automaticity, accuracy and prosody are achieved by all.

Wide reading reveals how writers connect across time, genre and tradition. Through knowledge of context and intertextuality, pupils learn that stories do not stand alone but belong to a shared cultural landscape in which ideas are inherited, contested and refined.

Reading for pleasure emerges as a long-term outcome of a curriculum that builds the competence, confidence and shared cultural entitlement required for all aspects of English to become genuinely enjoyable.” Archived from David Didau (Substack) on June 19, 2026 by Tim.
